results.title: Discovered Materials Raises $9M for AI-Powered Materials Discovery | Deal4Business posted on the topic | LinkedIn
results.content:
Deeptech startup Discovered Materials has raised $9 million (approximately ₹85 crore) in a seed funding round led by Lightspeed India Partners, with participation from Y Combinator, Peak XV Partners and others.
Founded by IIT Madras alumni Akash Ramdas and Advaith Sridhar, the San Francisco-based startup is building AI systems that can accelerate the materials discovery process from simulation and synthesis to laboratory validation.
The fresh capital will be used to expand the team, build laboratory infrastructure and advance its AI agents, with an initial focus on materials for advanced semiconductor applications.
Read full news here: [...] Discovered Materials has raised a $9 million seed round to find materials that let computer chips run cooler.
TechCrunch reported on August 10 that Lightspeed India Partners led the round, with Peak XV Partners and angels including Paul Graham and Gokul Rajaram also investing. The startup came out of Y Combinator.
The pitch: point AI agents at one narrow problem instead of materials discovery broadly. Cofounder Advaith Sridhar says the system runs thousands of guesses a day, compared to the roughly 20 a day his cofounder Akash Ramdas managed by hand during his materials science PhD at Stanford. Discovered Materials, a startup developing artificial intelligence agents to discover new materials for semiconductor chips, has raised USD 9 million, or approximately Rs 85 crore, in a seed funding round led by Lightspeed India Partners, according to a media report. [...] Y Combinator, Peak XV Partners and angel investors including Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram and Anthropic executive Thariq Shihipar also participated in the funding round.

The company will use the capital to expand its team and laboratory operations and scale its artificial intelligence research agents. Its technology aims to reduce the time required to identify, simulate and test materials used in semiconductor manufacturing.

Discovered Materials has released hundreds of new materials identified by artificial intelligence models. It has also introduced Material Discovery Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate artificial intelligence agents on real-world semiconductor materials problems. [...] Discovered Materials was founded by IIT Madras alumni Advaith Sridhar and Akash Ramdas. Ramdas holds a doctorate in materials science from Stanford University and has spent 11 years researching materials for semiconductor chips. Sridhar studied artificial intelligence at Carnegie Mellon University and previously worked on artificial intelligence models and agents at Persona AI and Luma Labs.

The company said its agents work across simulation, synthesis and experimental validation to help researchers identify promising materials faster and move them closer to commercial semiconductor production.

results.title: Discovered Materials is playing AI whack-a-mole to hunt cooler chips
results.content:
Tim Fernholz

Chips running AI workloads are too hot: That’s one reason why data centers consume so much electricity and require cooling systems. And, inevitably, entrepreneurs are turning to AI to solve the problem it created.

Discovered Materials is the latest, with plans to use swarms of AI agents to find new materials that can be used to build more efficient integrated circuits. The startup said it recently closed a $9 million seed round from Lightspeed India Partners after emerging from from Y Combinator, with investment from Peak XV Partners and angel investors Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram, and Thariq Shihipar. [...] One challenge is the engineering trade-space: If they find a material that might reduce heat generation or improve dissipation, it might be too difficult to actually manufacture a chip out of it, or its electrical properties are compromised.

“It’s a bit of playing whack-a-mole with atomic structures,” Hemant Mohapatra, the Lightspeed partner who led this round, told TechCrunch. “A material is only useful in the real world if all of them converge at once, which is what makes this a really interesting search problem.”
